source: Prescribed Material for the Leaving Certificate English Examination in 2027 (Department of Education circular, 27 February 2025): https://www.curriculumonline.ie/getmedia/ee4aa8b9-06c6-4091-974b-ea444dbae0af/Prescribed-Material-for-the-Leaving-Certificate-English-Examination-2027.pdf
rules: At Higher Level you study three texts for the comparative, from the prescribed list, in the modes set for your year.
For 2027 the Higher Level modes are Theme or Issue, Cultural Context, and General Vision and Viewpoint. All three are on the 2027 paper: you answer on one.
A single 70-mark question needs at least two of your texts; a 30 + 40 question needs one text in part (a) and the two others in part (b).
A Shakespeare play must be one of your Higher Level texts: as your single text or as one of your comparative texts. If Othello is in your comparative, your single text has to be another text.
A film can be one of your texts, and it should be discussed as a film: what we see and hear, not just what happens. You may refer to only one film in all your Paper 2 answers.
You can't reuse your single text in the comparative. Using a text that isn't prescribed, or the wrong combination, costs a third of a 70-mark answer.

criteria.name: Clarity of purpose
criteria.what: Engagement with the set task: relevance, focus, originality, freshness, evidence of critical literacy, clear aim, understanding of genre.
criteria.do: Answer the exact question asked, in the mode asked, from your first sentence to your last.
criteria.comp: For the comparative: understanding of the mode, focus on the exact task set, and effective comparison within the mode.

criteria.name: Coherence of delivery
criteria.what: Ability to sustain the response over the entire answer: continuity of argument, sequencing, management of ideas, choice of reference, use of examples, engagement with texts, control of register and shape.
criteria.do: Build every paragraph the same way (PACE) and compare the texts inside each paragraph, never one text after another.
criteria.comp: For the comparative: a sustained comparative focus, ideas managed and sequenced, apt use of examples.

criteria.name: Efficiency of language use
criteria.what: Management and control of language to achieve clear communication: vocabulary, syntax, sentence patterns, punctuation appropriate to the register, use of lively interesting phrasing, energy, style, fluency.
criteria.do: Use the language of comparison (similarly, in contrast, to a far greater extent) and the words of the mode.
criteria.comp: For the comparative: fluency, quality of expression, and the use of comparative language.

criteria.name: Accuracy of mechanics
criteria.what: Spelling and grammar: appropriate levels of accuracy in spelling and grammatical patterns appropriate to the register.
criteria.do: Spell the titles, authors and characters right, every time.
criteria.comp: For the comparative: accuracy of mechanics, the same as in any answer: spelling, grammar and punctuation, and the titles and names spelt right.

marks.note: These are the SEC's criteria for assessment, used for every answer on both English papers.
marks.primacy: Your marks for Coherence (C) and Language (L) can never be higher than your mark for Purpose (P). If you don't answer the question asked, in the mode asked, nothing else can make up for it.
marks.single: A single 70-mark question is marked on each criterion separately: P out of 21, C out of 21, L out of 21, M out of 7.
marks.splitText: A two-part question gets one mark for each part, judged against all four criteria together: part (a) out of 30, on one text; part (b) out of 40, comparing two other texts.
reward: Comparing and/or contrasting: similarities and differences, in both content and style.
Describing and analysing the texts in the light of the mode.
Making connections between similar aspects of the texts, and recognising differences.
Showing that similarities and differences need to be qualified (to what extent?).
Grounding your answer in key moments: you don't have to cover the whole text.
Showing awareness of yourself as a reader: your reactions, responses and involvement.
The quality of the comparative writing and apt reference to the texts.
marks.rewardSource: From the "General" note printed before the comparative in every SEC marking scheme, 2012–2026, and the instructions under each question.

modes.name: Theme or Issue
modes.what: A theme is a big idea a text keeps returning to, like power, freedom or courage. You compare how each text presents it, how it develops through key moments, and what each text finally says about it.
ask: How is the theme introduced at the start?
Which characters carry it, and how do they change?
Is it resolved at the end, and how?
What is the writer's (or director's) view of it?
Which text explores it most powerfully, and why?
modes.hook: Theme: the big idea. Ask what each text SAYS about it, not just that it's there.

official.quote: Comparing texts on a prescribed theme(s). These would have to be themes which were pervasive and central to the texts chosen for study.
official.src: Department of Education, Guidelines for Teachers of English (Leaving Certificate), Approaches to the Comparative Study of Texts

modes.name: Cultural Context
modes.what: The world of the text: the society its characters live in, its values, rules and power structures, and how that world shapes their lives and choices.
ask: Who holds power, and how do they use it?
What does this society value: money, status, reputation, faith?
What roles do men and women have? What is marriage for?
What part do religion, the law and institutions play?
Do characters conform or rebel, and what does it cost them?
Would you want to live in this world?
modes.hook: Cultural context: the WORLD of the text. Who has power, what's valued, what's allowed.

official.quote: Compare texts focusing on social rituals, values, and attitudes. This is not to be seen as a sociological study of the texts. It means taking some perspectives which enable the students to understand the kind of values and structures with which people contend.
official.src: Department of Education, Guidelines for Teachers of English (Leaving Certificate), Approaches to the Comparative Study of Texts

modes.name: General Vision and Viewpoint
modes.what: The text's outlook on life: is it bleak, hopeful or somewhere between? You trace the light and dark moments, especially the opening and the ending, and say what view of people and society the text leaves you with, and how the writer or director shapes that view.
ask: What is the outlook at the opening?
Which moments are light, and which are dark?
Does the outlook change, and when?
How does it end, and what does the ending say about people?
How does the writer (or director: music, light, camera, voiceover) shape your view?
Is the vision bleak, hopeful or mixed overall?
modes.hook: Vision: the VIEW OF LIFE. Track light vs dark, and judge it on the ending.

official.quote: The broad outlook of the authors of the texts and/or of the texts themselves as interpreted and understood by the reader.
official.also: Compare texts from the standpoint of the view they offer on life. Is it optimistic or pessimistic? What aspects of life do they concentrate on and why? (Guidelines for Teachers of English)

structure.time: About 65 minutes for the 70-mark question (Paper 2 is 3 hours 20 minutes).
structure.length: Aim for an introduction, 4 or 5 comparative paragraphs and a conclusion: roughly 1,000 to 1,300 words.

parts.name: Introduction
parts.what: Answer the question in your first sentence. Name the three texts with their authors or director, and the mode. Say briefly where your answer is going.
parts.avoid: Don't open with 'In this essay I will'. Don't retell the plots.

parts.name: Comparative paragraphs
parts.what: One aspect of the question per paragraph. Compare the texts inside every paragraph using PACE, so each paragraph is a mini-essay that answers the question.
parts.avoid: Don't write one paragraph per text: that's three separate essays, not a comparison.

parts.name: Conclusion
parts.what: Answer the question again in light of everything you've shown. Name the most important similarity or difference. Give your own response: which text affected you most, and why.
parts.avoid: Don't add a new point you haven't argued.

pace.name: Point
pace.what: A comparative topic sentence that answers the question and names this paragraph's aspect.
pace.eg: In all three texts, power lies with those who can control others, but only in Othello is it seized through words alone.

pace.name: Anchor
pace.what: Anchor the point in a key moment from your first text: what happens, a short quote or detail, and what it shows.
pace.eg: In Sive, Mena agrees to the match because Seán Dóta's money will rid her house of Sive.

pace.name: Compare
pace.what: Link to your second and third texts with a comparative phrase, each anchored in a key moment: alike, different, or the same to a greater or lesser degree.
pace.eg: Similarly, in The Shawshank Redemption, Warden Norton's power rests on money: the prisoners' labour fills his safe. In contrast, Iago holds no high rank, yet he controls Othello completely through words.

pace.name: Evaluate
pace.what: Say what the comparison shows and tie it back to the question: which text goes furthest, and what it leaves you thinking.
pace.eg: Of the three, Othello offers the bleakest view of power, because Iago needs nothing but Othello's trust to destroy him.

structure.hook: PACE yourself: Point, Anchor, Compare, Evaluate. Every paragraph, every time.

language.name: Bringing in a key moment
items: This is crystallised in the moment when

Nowhere is this clearer than when

We see this most vividly when

items: As a result, the vision becomes

paper.time: Paper 2, Higher Level: 3 hours 20 minutes, 200 marks.

sections.name: Single Text
sections.what: Othello (or your other single text): answer one of two questions. No change for 2027.

sections.name: Comparative Study
sections.what: For 2027, questions on all three modes are on the paper: you answer on one mode. You pick one of the two questions on that mode; each is either a single 70-mark question or a question in two parts (30 + 40).

sections.name: Poetry
sections.what: Unseen poem (20): one of two questions. Prescribed poetry (50): for 2027, one of five questions (one extra).

paper.seventy: A single 70-mark question: refer to at least two texts. It is marked by the same criteria whether you use two texts or three.
paper.split: A two-part question: part (a) (30 marks) on one text, part (b) (40 marks) on two other texts. Part (b) doesn't have to link back to part (a).
